subject: Business Models
title: Outcome-Based Pricing
description: Learn Outcome-Based Pricing in one minute.

hook.text: Rolls-Royce doesn't sell jet engines. It sells 'power by the hour'—airlines pay per flight hour, not per engine.

buildup.text: Outcome-based pricing charges for results, not products. You pay for the value delivered, not the thing built.

discovery.text: This aligns incentives: Rolls-Royce makes more money when engines last longer and planes fly more.

twist.text: Outcome-based pricing requires trust and data. Both parties must agree on what 'the outcome' actually means.

climax.text: Consulting firms, SaaS companies, and even law firms are experimenting with paying for results, not hours.

punchline.text: Pay per flight hour, not per engine. Outcome pricing aligns cost with value.

quiz.question: What is Rolls-Royce's 'power by the hour' model?
options: Charging airlines per flight hour instead of selling engines

details.summary: Outcome-based pricing charges customers only for measurable results rather than inputs, services, or time. Instead of billing per hour or per unit, the provider shares the financial risk by tying payment to the value actually delivered to the customer.
details.whyItMatters: Outcome-based pricing aligns provider incentives with customer success. When Rolls-Royce charges per engine flying hour rather than per engine sold, both parties benefit when engines run longer and more reliably.
takeaways: Payment is tied to measurable outcomes like cost savings or performance gains
Risk shifts from the buyer to the provider who controls the outcome
Rolls-Royce's power-by-the-hour is a classic outcome-based model

faq.question: What industries commonly use outcome-based pricing?
faq.answer: Aerospace with power-by-the-hour engine contracts, healthcare with value-based care reimbursement, digital advertising with cost-per-acquisition, energy services with guaranteed savings contracts, and consulting with success-fee arrangements.

faq.question: What makes outcome-based pricing difficult to implement?
faq.answer: Defining and measuring outcomes objectively, attributing outcomes to the provider versus external factors, managing financial risk from variable revenue, longer sales cycles due to complex contract negotiations, and needing robust data systems to track performance.
